annotations.keyFindings: Fewer patients scored above the post-traumatic stress threshold at three months with a relative-written diary (14 of 81, 17 percent) than with usual care (23 of 83, 28 percent); anxiety and depression did not differ.
annotations.limitations: 164 patients in three units; 19 percent lost to follow-up; not powered for secondary outcomes; blinding of outcome assessment not reported.

annotations.keyFindings: Across eleven controlled studies the pooled reduction in patients' post-traumatic stress symptoms (standardised mean difference -0.31) was not seen once three high-risk studies were removed; only three studies used family-written diaries.
annotations.limitations: Search ended in 2022; heterogeneous timing of reading and instruments; few family-written diary studies.

annotations.keyFindings: Relatives used the diary to cope with powerlessness, wanted a short guide rather than instructions, and four of 19 removed pages before handing the diary over.
annotations.limitations: One hospital; relatives who agreed to talk; conversations after discharge only.

annotations.keyFindings: Distress rose during first reading (median 2 to 4 of 10) and settled within a week for 88 of 96 survivors; eight reported intrusive memories, mostly those with high post-traumatic stress scores before reading.
annotations.limitations: Single follow-up clinic; no comparison group; distress self-rated in front of the nurse.

annotations.keyFindings: Relatives with post-traumatic stress symptoms above threshold fell from 36 to 27 percent after a diary programme began, with a smaller difference once bereaved relatives were excluded.
annotations.limitations: Uncontrolled before-after comparison; about 40 percent non-response; responders more often spouses.

annotations.keyFindings: Recommends diaries after more than 72 hours of ventilation, writing by relatives, a written guide, rules on photographs and confidentiality, and clinician-supported reading; no recommendation on who should write.
annotations.limitations: Consensus of one regional network; evidence review methods described briefly.

annotations.keyFindings: A diary was started in 54 percent of 1,120 admissions: 31 percent when the family's language differed from the unit's and 38 percent without a regular visitor, against 61 percent otherwise.
annotations.limitations: Four units in one region; reasons for not offering a diary were not recorded.

claims.text: In a trial of 164 ventilated adults, 17 percent of patients with a relative-written diary and 28 percent with usual care scored above the post-traumatic stress threshold at three months.
claims.passage: 14 of 81 patients in the diary group and 23 of 83 in the usual care group scored above the threshold (17 versus 28 percent)
claims.interpretation: The best single estimate of effect in patients; one trial of moderate size, so the review should present it with its limits.

claims.text: Across eleven controlled studies, the pooled reduction in patients' post-traumatic stress symptoms with diaries did not survive removal of the studies at high risk of bias, and only three studies used family-written diaries.
claims.passage: the effect was not seen when the three studies at high risk of bias were removed
claims.interpretation: The pooled effect is fragile; the review should not present diaries as proven.

claims.text: First reading of a diary raised distress that settled within a week for 88 of 96 survivors, and intrusive memories after reading occurred mainly in patients with high post-traumatic stress scores beforehand.
claims.passage: returned to baseline within a week for 88 of 96 patients
claims.interpretation: Reading is usually tolerable but should follow a screen for post-traumatic stress symptoms.

claims.text: Diary uptake was 31 percent when the family's main language differed from the unit's language, against 61 percent for other families with a regular visitor.
claims.passage: Uptake was 31 percent when the family's main language differed from the unit's language
claims.interpretation: A diary programme can widen differences in who benefits; the review should cover who is offered a diary.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level: one randomised trial, one systematic review, two observational studies, one before-after comparison, one qualitative study and one consensus statement. The single trial of relative-written diaries found fewer patients above the post-traumatic stress threshold at three months, but the review's pooled effect in patients was fragile to risk of bias and included only three family-written diary studies. Effects in relatives rest on one uncontrolled comparison and mixed controlled results. First reading raises distress briefly and can trigger intrusive memories in patients who already have high symptoms. Uptake is lower for families with a different language or no regular visitor, and programmes lapse when the lead nurse leaves. A narrative review can state these findings with their certainty; it cannot settle whether family-written diaries work better than staff-written ones.
gradeRationale: One moderate-sized trial and a review whose pooled effect disappears when high-risk studies are removed, with indirectness for family-written diaries and imprecision in relatives; certainty that family-led diaries reduce post-traumatic stress symptoms is low, and very low for relatives.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.
